title: The tenth man
hookLine: ten travelers cross a river, count themselves, and find only nine
carry: you are the tenth: the self was never missing
last: NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.

lines: THEY WEEP FOR THE LOST ONE.
cards: Ten friends set out on a trip together, and they have to ford a fast river. They wade across, holding on to each other, and scramble up the far bank, soaked. The leader, to be safe, counts heads.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Nine. He counts again.
Nine. Someone's been swept away. Each of the others counts, and each gets nine too.
They sit down on the riverbank and weep for their lost friend.

teach.b: A traveler walking by asks what's wrong. They tell him: there were ten of us, and one has drowned. He looks at them, and counts.
Ten. He asks the leader to count again. Nine.
Then the traveler touches the leader on the shoulder and says: you are the tenth. That's the whole story. It's told in Advaita Vedanta texts because it shows how neti neti works in practice.
The leader wasn't missing. He was doing the counting, so he never counted himself. He was looking everywhere but at the looker.
And notice: nothing new was found. No one came out of the river. The grief ended the moment he recognized what had been there the whole time.
That's why jnana is called knowledge, not achievement. Hindu teachers say the atman, your real self, is never lost and never gained. You don't become the self.
You stop leaving it out of the count. So how do you practice it? Neti neti in real life is a kind of honest sorting.
When you feel, I am angry, look closer: anger is showing up, and something is aware of it. Not this.
When you think, I am a failure, look closer: a thought is showing up. Not this. You don't deny the anger or the thought.
You just stop counting them as the counter. What's left is the one who was looking. The Upanishads have a phrase for this recognition, and later teachers repeat it again and again: you are that.

how: Advaita Vedanta teachers often use the parable of the tenth man to show that self-knowledge isn't gaining something new but recognizing what was always present; students then practice discerning the witness from what it witnesses.

o: knowing yourself as the one aware, not what you notice
a habit of counting things to settle a busy mind
learning more and more facts about who you are

games.q: the tenth man — tap the pairs.
p: don't count the counted as the counter

s: in the story, the tenth friend is found downstream
no one was lost: the leader forgot to count himself.
the parable of the tenth man is used in Advaita Vedanta texts
teachers use it to show self-knowledge is recognition, not gain.
neti neti means denying that your thoughts and feelings exist
they're real; you just stop counting them as the one who is aware.

games.q: you're the leader. you've counted nine, three times. a traveler says there are ten of you. what's missing?
games.why: you are the tenth. the counter never counted himself.

practice: Count, like the leader on the riverbank: one, the body sitting; two, the breath; three, a sound in the room; four, a thought; five, whatever mood is here. Then pause and ask: who's counting?
Don't answer with a word; just turn toward the counter, the way the traveler turned the leader around, and when counting starts again, let it.

wordCard.voice: Jnana yoga, in practice. Neti neti sets aside what can be counted, the body, the thoughts, the moods, and turns you toward the counter. You are the tenth.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dashamas tvam asi, 'you are the tenth', the punchline of the Vedanta parable.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the tenth. The self was never missing; it was doing the counting. Day two seventy-five, counted.

sources.ref: the parable of the tenth man (Shankara, Upadeshasahasri; Vidyaranya, Panchadashi ch. 7)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi, you are that)
